Juvenile blackbird hit our balcony window and fell onto the floor. After a few minutes it was back on its feet. These are the last minutes of it calling out while trying to jump/fly onto some drying wires from a sack of soil he had been sitting on for over half an hour. Eventually it succeeded and flew away. Weak flight calls can be heard in the last seconds of the recording.
Interaction with the bird was minimal, I put out some water but it wasn't interested in it. Thawed berries and a cardboard box were ready to keep it safe overnight (cats regularly roam the area) but weren't necessary. Overall it took a little over an hour from hitting the window to flying away.

rmk: This clip offers a comparison between BLACKCAP and then GARDEN WARBLER (from 0:40). Both were singing in the same area. The Blackcap recording features two males that were 'song sparring' but, somewhat unfortunately, the Garden Warbler clip has a WILLOW WARBLER overlapping at 0:47 and then a CHAFFINCH at 0:51. The chief means for distinguishing between the Blackcap and Garden Warbler could be summarised as, for BLACKCAP, a more explosive song burst with 'spiky'  (heterogeneous) notes that, in these typical short bursts used by males when singing against each other, usually have a well defined finale.  GARDEN WARBLER has, if anything, a faster rate of singing but it sounds softer and more purring without a well-defined finale. Although Garden Warbler sings at a rapid pace, the pitch is slightly lower and the sound is more steady (homogeneous) than a Blackcap. The quality of Garden Warbler sound is hard to describe but it could be said to be a fast puttering?

rmk:
A Blackcap singing almost continuously. This habit is prevalent in spring when males seem to be motivated to sing more and for longer, presumably in a bid to attract a mate. Alternatively, the 'wall of sound' could be because they have a mate and now wish to use the maximum amount of song to deter other males from visiting the vicinity? 

Among this male's repertoire - and not uncommonly from among the repertoire of Blackcaps in Ireland - there is the occasional  phrase that sounds a bit like a Nightingale.  I know Nightingale song from Catalonia.  The phrase in question can be heard just after 0:10. A Buzzard calls at 1:03 (four calls over the next five seconds).

Blackcaps regularly mimic. One singer that, unfortunately, I failed to record, began his song with Blackbird phrases. So much so that I was astonished when he broke into typical voice and was not a Blackbird. In this recording, it strikes me that the opening three seconds could well be a sample of Robin. If you heard say, just the first three seconds, would you not think you were listening to a Robin?

rmk:
This is the same male that featured in XC552441. Unlike the latter recording, there is no rival singing in competition. This individual Blackcap has a trademark 'yodel' that it uses in almost all its verses. The yodel (for want of a better word) is included in this clip - but it was noticeably absent when the bird was involved in direct competition with a rival. The yodel (a kind of alternating change in scale, a bit like a boogie-woogie riff on a piano) can be heard at 0:07; 0:18; 0:30; 0:42. Unlike in XC552441, the Blackcap had largely ceased its mimicry of Blackbird. Nonetheless, you can again here Blackbird samples at 0:15 and 0:26. For some reason, the Blackbird samples from this passage of singing are much more embedded in the overall composition - and could easily be overlooked. 

From this and other Blackcaps I sometimes hear a fleeting haunting sound that reminds me of Nightingale. I do not know if the birds are actually copying Nightingales - that they presumably hear when the two species overlap on migration in Spain and maybe southern France - or create the sound themselves. The sound I mean is at 0:38 and lasts roughly two seconds. 

Other species in the clip are: Wren (0:10) and Great Tit (0:13; 0:20; 0:26).

loc: Ireland (near  Bangor), Ards and North Down, Northern Ireland
rmk:
This recording is an extract from several hours of vocal arm-wrestling between two rival male Blackcaps. Competition seems to be at maximum intensity, heightened further because at least one female Blackcap was in the area. Maybe she was partnered to one of the males? Both males had been in the area for over a fortnight. Initially - and presumably before any female arrived - the song was less prolonged and lacked much mimicry of other species.  Competition seems to have spurred the males to 'raise their game'. Hence the song bursts are longer and more sustained, with bits of mimicry included for embellishment. Six verses are on the clip. The duration of most exceeds five or six seconds, which is typical of song bursts when the birds first arrive in early April (such as XC552444).  Two bursts are over ten seconds; one lasts 26 seconds (from 1:03).  Mimicry of Blackbird can be heard at 0:34-36 (start of third verse); 0:42-44 (start of fourth verse); 0:52-54 (end of fourth verse). In these - and other instances, not on the clip - mimicry is either at the beginning or end of a song burst.  The verbal battle has the briefest of breaks. I assume the breaks are only because one male is pausing to check if its rival is still singing. Unlike other songbirds that indulge in singing contests, Blackcaps sing against each other and overlap their efforts. They do not take it in turns - as Robins, Dunnocks, Blackbirds and others do. The same Blackcap can be heard at XC552452 - but singing on his own, when he seems less animated. The rival either went quiet or moved elsewhere. 

A Woodpigeon utters its classic broadcast sequence at 0:15 until the 24th second.

rmk: Typical song bursts from a male Blackcap. The bird stayed hidden among deciduous trees at about 6 m off the ground.  The pattern of each phrase is fairly consistent, even though the fine print of each delivery varies a little. The opening notes are gappy and disconnected. The main burst comes as a blast of notes that hit a higher pitch. The finale - that comes on quickly - sometimes contains two melodic notes [such as at the end of 0:31 and in subsequent bursts] that crash into each other and could be made to fit the words 'see-who'. Blackcaps are occasional mimics and this bird throws in a Blackbird-like note as an introductory note. You can hear it best at 0:36 but it is also fairly clear at 0:11 and 0:43.

rmk: Drumming from a male Great Spotted Woodpecker. This bird's partner was incubating in a nest hole approximately 30m away - so it might have heard the drumming from inside the nest cavity?  The clip begins with a WILLOW WARBLER (over the first three seconds, already singing at 0:01)  and the same Willow Warbler can be heard subsequently, such as at 0:36 and 0:46. At 0:03, the first drum (the first of nine) can be heard. Note that the quality of each drum can vary a little. For example, some drums are shorter than others, such at 0:41. At 0:05 a WREN sings. It sings again at 0:21 but a Willow Warbler overlaps the start of the song. At 0:02 a BLACKBIRD sings. It sings throughout most of the first half of the recording; a particularly clear piece of Blackbird starts at the end of 0:24 and is good over the 25th and 26th seconds. At 0:16 a ROBIN sings (and sings again later at 0:28, accompanied, shortly after, by wing-beats). The first clear burst of CHAFFINCH song commences at 0:25 (less clear song comes earlier at 0:07). However, at 1:25 and to the end of the clip you can hear the CHAFFINCH delivering its 'mark time' alternative to its song by broadcasting its (to my ears) 'de-feat' couplet endlessly.  Other background sounds are COMMON GULL calls at 0:49 and COOT at 1:05 (several times thereafter).

rmk: I consider this an important example of Great Tit mimicking other species that it knows to be present in its territory and, through copying their voice, intentionally drawing them in to join with the Great Tit in observing a trespasser, predator or anything that the Great Tit regards as worth investigating. In this instance, I am the curiosity. The recording begins (during the first two seconds) with a popular 'pink, pink' refrain that precedes Great Tit's diagnostic 'revving' [please read detailed comments of XC202429 to establish what I mean by 'revving']. The 'pink, pink' seems to function as a copy of the same note commonly used by Chaffinch. At 0:04, the 'pink, pink' is dropped and only revving is uttered. After 0:04 (but closer to the fifth second) a faint Blue Tit call (this tuneful note serves as both song and alarm call) is heard in the background. Just after 0:07, the Great Tit delivers 'pink, pink, pink'. In the following few seconds the Great Tit moved farther off but, at 0:11, it prefaces revving with the trill of a Long-tailed Tit. Indeed, Long-tailed Tits were in the immediate area and, shortly after, both they and more Blue and Coal Tits all appeared like rats responding to the summons of the 'Pied Piper' Great Tit.
First recording with Zoom H5 & Rode NTG8

Three or four shallow waterfowl impoundments partially flooded in the winter.

#Editing#
Adobe Audition. Butterworth high-pass filter, cutoff 500 hz, order 3

#Equipment#
Fostex FR-2 digital recorder with Sennheiser microphone and Telinga pro 22" parabolic reflector.

Sinds lang heb ik een zwak voor de zang van de Noordse Nachtegaal, Sprosser in het Duits. Meer nog dan onze gewone Nachtegaal spreekt zijn zang mij aan: voller en lager van klank, wat trager en met karakteristieke ratels aan het eind van elke zangstrofe. Toen ik dan in de gelegenheid was om met een aantal collega's van Natuurmonumenten een bezoek brengen aan het dal van de Peene in voormalig Oost Duitsland, heb ik die kans gegrepen om zijn zang op te nemen. Het bezoek was van 10-14 juni 2005, van alle 4 overnachtingen heb ik een deel gewijd aan het opnemen van geluiden. Naast de zang van ze soort, heb ik ook andere soorten opgenomen, maar op vrijwel alle opnames zijn ook Sprosser te horen. De opnames zijn gemaakt rond onze verblijfplaats in GUtzkow. In de directe omgeving hiervan zijn verschillende voorbeelden aanwezig van voormalige landbouwgebieden, die nu een natuurbestemming hebben gekregen, het doel van het werkbezoek.

rmk: Song from an adult Song Thrush (aged because the bird was in full view and allowed scrutiny of the relevant part of the wing to determine its age).  Apart from the Song Thrush, the only other easily discernible calls are monosyllabic notes interjected by a House Sparrow, such as at 0:02, 0:06 and 0:09.  Sometimes I notice that  Song Thrushes on Inishbofin (at least fifteen singing males since around 2014, previously just two during 2007-2012 when the the species suffered severe nest predation from Magpies ... since removed) do not indulge in as much 'overt' repetition as I hear from Song Thrushes in eastern Ireland.  Nonetheless, repetition is a hallmark of Inishbofin Song Thrushes too (a typical example is the four repetitions starting just before 0:18) but it can be less obvious. By this I mean that the repeated note may be less ear-catching because it is a high note or a note that is not especially strident - or because the songster intersperses a different note during a repeated sequence, thereby 'masking'  the repeated series. An example of a rogue note breaking up a sequence can be heard after 0:46 where two high notes are repeated but are then followed with a different note (the bird drops the pitch to create this note)  before it repeats the original high note for a third time. Note: the full sequence of two high notes, the dropped note, then the same high note again, is contained with a short space of just two seconds, from the 46th to the 48th second.

rmk: The recording features not just call notes from a juvenile Song Thrush but also calls from a juvenile Blackbird. In fact, there are more sounds from the Blackbird than the Song Thrush. I should explain the circumstances. I am very interested in all sounds made by all ages of Song Thrushes and Blackbirds. However, it seems somewhat peculiar that juvenile Blackbirds - when they are fledged but not yet independent of their parents, who continue to feed them - are very vocal, whereas Song Thrushes of equivalent age emit a much more limited range of sounds. In fact, possibly just one note. That note, more or less, seems to be the same note that becomes the standard 'tix' flight note used by all subsequent ages of Song Thrush. I would be interested to hear from anyone that can add more information about the range of calls (if there is a range!) given by juvenile Song Thrushes in their pre-independence days. The recording was made beside a dense thicket of Sycamore, albeit only 3m wide and 2m tall, on Inishbofin, off the coast of Co. Galway. Three fledged Song Thrushes were hiding in the tree, as well as one fledged Blackbird. For the purposes of the recording, I could not see the Blackbird but I could see one of the Song Thrushes. Its single high-pitched note interjects among the Blackbird's loud, staccato outbursts. The Song Thrush can be heard at 0:12, 0:13, 0:21, 0:26, 0:31, 0:43, 0:50, 0:52 and 0:53. A few other monosyllables might also have come from the Song Thrush but I can only vouch for those that are listed in the timestamps. Also in the background, a Wren can be heard, such as after 0:23, 0:34 and 0:47.
